Part III · Chapter 6

Intent first

Draft

Run on 2026-11-23 16:31 UTC+01:00 by the reference verifier of the zayn command, release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), against the law at version 3.17: the verifier gave the expected answer on 11 of 11 declarations.

Each declaration on this page was checked as a file by the verifier's JavaScript reference, the one the zayn command is held to, under Node 22.20.0. Every report printed below is the one that run gave. The lines that begin with //--> state the answer the page expects, and the build fails on any other.

Intent first is the rule Zayn rests on: an interface is declared from what its user is doing, and a control on a screen is what that intent becomes in one medium. In this chapter I write a first declaration, three lines long, and I name the words it is made of. Then I give the verbs, all 22 of them, and I show what the verifier answers when a word is outside them, when a flow names no intent, when an element of an interface answers to no verb, and when a declaration starts from a widget.

Three words first. The law is Zayn's constitution for interfaces: 7 articles, and 123 numbered rules that derive from them, kept as data. Their numbers run to 130: the law does not give again the number of a rule it merged into another, nor a number it reserved. The verifier is the program that reads a declaration and checks it against the law. A widget is a drawn control or container: a button, a card, a table.

The field

React, for one, builds an interface from the thing drawn. Its Quick Start says that apps "are made out of components", and that a component is a piece of the interface with its own logic and its own appearance. The first word written is the name of a thing on a screen.

The field has also started from the other end. In 2014 a working group of the W3C published a note on task models, which "describe the logical activities" a user carries out to reach a goal, and it built its exchange format on a notation named ConcurTaskTrees. A companion note describes an abstract interface, written with no reference to how it is implemented and independent of any modality, graphical, vocal or haptic. Both are Working Group Notes, and the first says in its own status that the group stopped taking it toward a W3C Recommendation.

So the idea of starting from what the user does is in the field's record. It stands there as a description that tools exchange. Each of these pages was read at its source on 23 November 2026, and Appendix F lists them.

The principle

An interface is declared from what its user is doing, in a closed set of verbs: a widget is what an intent becomes in a medium, never where a declaration starts.

The law holds the inversion as its second article.

Article IIIntent Over Mechanics

Interaction starts from what the human is trying to do — discover, focus, read, select, act, recover — and widgets are consequences of intent, never primitives. Selection never implies execution; a flow that traps is unconstitutional.

Printed from the law's data, version 3.17.

The article's sentence is prose: its last word, recover, is in no list. The list that the verifier holds comes below.

The Zayn site says in one sentence what the other starting point costs: "When the unit of declaration is a widget, a tool can check only the widget."

The first declaration

Here is the home screen of a ledger of invoices, declared.

Clean! The verifier found nothing to report, and it handed back the number 0. That number is the exit code, what a command returns when it ends. A team's build, the chain of commands that turns its sources into a product, reads it to know whether to go on.

Read the three lines. DEFINE opens every declaration. SCREEN is its kind: a place where a user can be. invoices_home is its name. Between the parentheses come its fields, and this one has a single field, SATISFIES, with the list of what the user does here. Nothing in the three lines says list, table, button or colour.

To run it yourself, save the lines in a file and give the file to the verifier: zayn check invoices.zayn. Chapter 25 installs the command, and the testbench of the Zayn site checks a declaration in the browser with nothing installed. The line that begins with //--> is a comment, which the verifier skips: it states the answer this page expects, and the book's build fails if the verifier gives another.

A second field carries the rest of the idea.

An INTENT_FLOW is a flow: the intents a user goes through, under one name. SATISFIES says what the surface lets the user do. ALWAYS_REACHABLE says what the user can get to at any step of it. Chapter 8 shows what the verifier does with a flow that acts and keeps nothing within reach.

The verbs, in their families

The words between the brackets are not free. They are the verbs of the law, and the law holds them in 6 families.

FamilyIts verbsWhat its verbs keep true
orientingDISCOVER UNDERSTAND LOCATEDiscovery must be satisfiable at every entry point.
attentionFOCUS FILTER COMPAREAn active filter is visible state; focus and discovery cannot both be at maximum.
informationREAD SCAN SCROLL ZOOMA read surface that silently acts is an intent violation.
selectionSELECT HIGHLIGHT PREVIEW MARKSelection expresses interest, never commitment.
actionACT CONFIRM CANCEL UNDOEvery act has a reachable undo, or declares why it cannot.
continuityPAUSE RESUME RETRY EXITPause, resume, and exit are always reachable; a trapped flow is unconstitutional.

Printed from the law's data, version 3.17.

Read the right column. Each family carries one sentence that its verbs must keep true in every declaration: its invariant. Several refusals of this book come from those sentences. A screen that reads and acts breaks the invariant of information. A flow where selecting carries out the act breaks the invariant of selection. Chapter 8 runs the invariants of action and of continuity. An invariant is the law's sentence, and what the verifier checks of it can be narrower: each chapter says which part a check decides.

If you come from the Zayn site, you met the same verbs grouped by what a user is busy with: understanding, deciding, acting, recovering. The families are the law's own grouping, and chapter 13 gives the other.

A word outside the verbs

What happens when a declaration uses a word that is not on the list? Here is a word a first draft reaches for.

Refused, and the exit code is 1! The report's first line gives the place, invoices.zayn:2, the severity, error, the code, UNKNOWN_INTENT, and what it is about. Its second line gives the reason. Its third line gives the law: Article II, the one printed above, and no rule, because the law has no numbered rule for this and the verifier claims none.

Why is NAVIGATE not a verb? Because it hides two intents. A user who navigates is going to a place they know, which is LOCATE, or is finding out which places exist, which is DISCOVER. The declaration has to say which, and only its author knows. The second plate of this chapter is the repair for the first case.

I keep the list closed on purpose. A medium is where an interface reaches its user: a screen, a voice, a printed page. A new medium brings new drawings of the same verbs: a voice has no button, and its user still acts. The grammar's own note says of a medium that seems to need a new verb that it "has misread its medium".

A flow that names no intent

From the file alone, the verifier asks one kind of declaration for its SATISFIES: the INTENT_FLOW, a flow. Here is one that says only what stays within reach.

A finding, and the exit code is 0. Look at the severity on the first line: warning. A warning is a finding that lets the declaration pass. An error is a refusal. The report's second line says it: "An INTENT_FLOW declares no intents." The build goes on. The lawful shape is the second plate of this chapter: a flow with its SATISFIES.

An element with no verb

Now what the inversion asks of every element. Each one answers to a verb, or it has no reason to be there.

A declaration cannot know which elements exist on a screen: it does not draw the screen. So the verifier is told. The list of elements is given to it in a small file, a symbol table, and the check is made at level 3, the first level where the verifier is given more than the declaration. A COMPONENT is a second kind of declaration: a part of a surface with a meaning of its own.

Refused, and this time the third line cites a rule: Rule 130. The first line has no line number, because the element is in the inventory and not in the file. The report's sentence says "a declared element": it means an element that the inventory says exists.

Rule 130Every Element Serves an Intent
Article
II · Intent Over Mechanics
Set
29 · Declaration Governance
Tier
machine
Cited by
INTENT_ORPHAN
Why
An element no intent asks for competes with the ones that matter (Article I) and answers a question nobody put. The person spends attention deciding it is irrelevant, or takes it for a choice. Being able to name the intent is the cheapest test an element has to pass, and an element that cannot pass it is mechanics, which Article II puts below intent.

Printed from the law's data, version 3.17.

A card gives the rule's article, its set, which is a group of rules on one subject, and its tier, a word the law files each rule under and that chapter 17 reads.

The rule's text gives two repairs: the element "is removed, or the intent it was always meant to serve is declared". Here is the second.

Clean. The rule says of this repair that declaring an element "is the moment the element is first asked what it is for".

A kind for the widget

One more word that a first draft reaches for.

A warning, and the exit code is 0: the language has no kind named WIDGET, and the verifier reports the word where it is written. The report names two words, WIDGET and USER: they are the two kinds the language knows of and leaves out. Any other word in the place of a kind is read as another language's declaration and passed over whole, as chapter 7's exercise shows. The repair names what the user does with the figures and leaves the card to the drawing.

Clean. Card or table is the drawing's business.

The decision, and what was refused

What I refused

I refused a kind for the widget. A widget is a consequence of an intent. A declaration that could name one would start from the drawing, and the language would have two starting points.

I refused one more verb. The verbs are a closed list, and NAVIGATE is a word it turns away. A closed list is what makes the rest countable: which verbs a medium carries, which rules speak of which verb.

I refused to leave the founding check outside the law. The verifier reported an element that answers to no verb before any numbered rule said so. On 2 November 2026 the check was given its rule, number 130, and the law's record says that the order was reversed: the check came first.

The court

The court of a chapter is what proves it. Here it is a set of fixtures from Zayn's conformance suite: declarations kept with the answer each must get. The build ran each fixture below in the snapshot of Zayn and compared its answer with the suite's manifest, its list of expected answers.

One pair stands in the box, expression-orphan and the same file repaired: the same check one layer down, citing Article II and no rule, for a declaration that says how its values should be perceived and says nothing of what its user is doing. The plates of this chapter repair the defects of the other fixtures.

Where the field leads

The field leads in what a task model can say. The W3C note describes tasks with the order between them and their decomposition into subtasks: one task enables another, two tasks are a choice, one suspends another. A declaration of Zayn lists the intents of a surface and names a wizard's steps. The operators between tasks, a choice, an interruption, are what the task model adds.

And a framework builds the screen. A declaration builds none: a team still draws its interface with the framework it has, and Zayn checks what was declared before the drawing begins.

Where it stands

  • builtthe 22 verbs in 6 families, each with its invariant, as data of the law; a word outside them refused from the file alone; an element that answers to no verb refused at level 3, against an inventory the verifier is given, under Rule 130
  • designedthe tables that say which control follows from which intent in each medium; the inventory of elements computed from a project in place of being given
  • nextthe law served to an AI model while it generates

Built means that it ran on this page or runs in Zayn's repository at the commit named under the title. Designed means that it is specified, and that its build comes after. Next names the direction.

Starting from intent makes checkable what a declaration states: its verbs, what it keeps within reach, its steps, from the file alone and before anything is drawn. That every element answers to a verb is decided at level 3, when the verifier is given the list of elements. At level 3, an element answers to a verb when a declaration carries its name and satisfies one.

In your hands

Here is a first draft written in the words of mechanics, with a form that points at its flow, and the inventory of the screen. A FORM is a third kind of declaration: a surface where a user enters something.

Cover the report under the declaration. Write the codes you expect, and how many times each. Then compare.

Now say each word as a verb of the law, and check the file again with the inventory of the screen, at level 3: zayn check lookup.zayn --level 3 --symbols screen.json. The inventory holds two elements, the form and a banner. Write what you expect first. Try before you read on.

Searching a list is narrowing it, which is FILTER. Going to an invoice the user knows is LOCATE. Viewing it is READ. And two elements are reported. The banner you expected. The form is the surprise: it names its flow, and the flow is lawful. Go on until the verifier answers clean and every line of your file is true. Do not give the banner a verb it does not serve: the declaration would be untrue.

Here is a form the verifier accepts, with the banner gone from the screen.

It is clean, and the form says twice what it is for: once by naming its flow, once by a verb of its own. For the trace, the verifier reads the second. Should an element that names its flow answer through it?

A verb says what a user does. The next chapter gives the 10 kinds of declaration that say where, and the whole grammar on one page.

Part III · Chapter 7

Ten declarations, one grammar

Draft

Run on 2026-11-23 16:31 UTC+01:00 by the reference verifier of the zayn command, release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), against the law at version 3.17: the verifier gave the expected answer on 14 of 14 declarations.

Each declaration on this page was checked as a file by the verifier's JavaScript reference, the one the zayn command is held to, under Node 22.20.0. Every report printed below is the one that run gave. The lines that begin with //--> state the answer the page expects, and the build fails on any other.

The grammar of Zayn is the set of rules that say what a declaration may be made of. It fits on one page, and this chapter is that page. I give the grammar in five sentences. I show each of the 10 kinds of declaration once, in files the verifier accepts. Then I make the grammar refuse: a field it does not know, a field in the wrong place, a field written twice, a value from outside a closed list.

Chapter 6 gave the verbs and two of the fields every kind carries, SATISFIES and ALWAYS_REACHABLE. The verifier is the program that checks a declaration against the law, Zayn's constitution for interfaces.

The field

The field has written languages that describe an interface above the widget, and it has written them for a long time. XForms, a W3C Recommendation of 2009, describes a form with an architecture that "separates presentation, purpose and content", and names its controls by purpose: an input, a choice of one, a trigger. UIML, an OASIS specification of the same year, calls itself a meta-language "for describing user interfaces". SCXML, a W3C Recommendation of 2015, is a language of state machines: what state a system is in, and which events move it.

More recently the field is writing names for the values of a drawing. The Design Tokens format, a draft report of its community group, defines a token as information with "a human readable name", and its types include a colour, a dimension and a font family.

Each of these is a description that a tool reads. Each was read at its source on 23 November 2026, and Appendix F lists them.

The principle

A declaration is made of two sorts of words: the names its author chooses, and the words the language holds. The second sort is a closed list, and each word of it has its place.

The verifier's contract gives the reason in one clause: "a vocabulary that anyone may extend cannot be checked".

The grammar, in five sentences

A file is a list of declarations, and of comments that begin with // and run to the end of the line.

A declaration is the word DEFINE, a kind, a name, and its fields between parentheses, separated by commas.

A field is a keyword followed by a list of names between square brackets, or by one value: a name, a text between quotes, a number, true or false.

The order of the fields is free, a field appears once in a declaration, and a name is used once within a kind.

Nothing nests: the value of a field is never another declaration.

That is all of it. The words in capitals belong to the language and are written in capitals. The other words are yours, except the values of the closed lists, which this chapter gives further down.

The kinds, in three files

Three kinds say how a user moves.

An INTENT_FLOW is a flow: the intents a user goes through, under one name. The verifier reads the list as a set: which verbs it holds. A FORM is a surface where a user enters something, and it names the flow it serves. From the file alone that is enough; chapter 6's exercise showed what an inventory asks of it at level 3, a verb of its own. A WIZARD is a flow with named steps in order.

Four kinds say where a user is.

A SCREEN is a place a user can be. A COMPONENT is a part of a surface with a meaning of its own: it says what a user does with it, and never what it looks like. A NAV_GRAPH says how surfaces connect. In a menu, each entry is one NAV_GRAPH, and chapter 26 declares a whole menu. A WORLD_VIEW is a space with things in it, seen from a stated point.

The last three kinds are a control, a message and a culture.

An INTERACTION stands for one control and can state its role, the promise the control makes. A FEEDBACK is what the system says back, and one that takes a tone or moves must report a state. A VIBE is a culture of use: how dense, on which medium, with what motion. Chapter 14 is about cultures.

Three files, 10 kinds, and the verifier accepts all three!

A field it does not know

Now the refusals. The first is the plainest: a keyword that is not the language's.

Refused, at line 3. The finding has two lines: what was found, and why. It cites no law, because no rule of the law is needed to say that a word is not in the grammar. The repair is to take the line out. A declaration has no word for a colour: red is the drawing's business, and what red would mean is said another way, which the last refusal of this chapter shows.

A field in the wrong place

A known field can sit on a kind that does not carry it. Every kind carries SATISFIES, ALWAYS_REACHABLE, SIGNALS and ACTOR. Beyond those, each kind has its own fields.

KindThe fields it carries, beyond those every kind carries
INTENT_FLOW SCREEN COMPONENTnone of its own
FORMINTENT_FLOW
WIZARDSTEPS
NAV_GRAPHVISIBLE_STATE LABEL TARGET ENTRIES
WORLD_VIEWPERSPECTIVE VISIBLE_ENTITIES
INTERACTIONROLE
FEEDBACKTONE REPORTS MOTION
VIBEDENSITY SURFACE_AS MOTION REPORTS SUPPRESSES

Printed from the language specification, version 1.7.

Refused, and the finding says where the field belongs: TONE is a message's field. A tone is how the system speaks, and a screen does not speak. The repair gives the tone to a message.

Clean. Before this check existed, a field on the wrong kind was read by nothing and reported by nothing, and its author believed it was working. The table says where a field belongs. The verifier also reads some fields wherever they sit, so they pass on any kind: STEPS (a declaration that carries it is read as having steps), INTENT_FLOW (its name is looked up wherever it is written), VISIBLE_STATE and VISIBLE_ENTITIES (gathered from the whole file). That is why chapter 9 writes VISIBLE_STATE on a SCREEN.

A field takes a list in brackets, or one value. SATISFIES, ALWAYS_REACHABLE and SUPPRESSES take a list of verbs. STEPS, VISIBLE_STATE, VISIBLE_ENTITIES, REPORTS and ENTRIES take a list of names, and the names of ENTRIES are those of other NAV_GRAPH declarations, in the order the menu shows them. INTENT_FLOW, TARGET and ACTOR take one name; the verifier looks up the name of an INTENT_FLOW in the file, and the specification says of TARGET and ENTRIES that neither "is resolved against the surfaces of the system". LABEL takes words in quotation marks. DENSITY and MOTION take one word of the author's: the specification gives compact and comfortable as examples of the first, and says of the second that "none is lawful and common". The other fields take their words from closed lists, which the last refusals of this chapter show.

A field written twice

Refused, at the second copy. The verifier does not merge the two lists and does not keep the last one. Which of the two did the author mean? It asks. The repair writes the list once.

Clean.

A value outside a closed list

Beside the verbs, 5 fields take their value from a closed list. Here they are, with every value each one admits.

FieldOnThe values it admits, and no others
PERSPECTIVEWORLD_VIEWtop_down isometric first_person side_scroll
TONEFEEDBACKcelebratory cautionary critical neutral informational
SURFACE_ASVIBEvisual auditory voice haptic print luminous signage machine spatial terminal
SIGNALSany declarationsuccess warning danger info muted
ROLEINTERACTIONinert navigate reversible irreversible proposal

Printed from the language specification, version 1.7.

A word outside a list is refused, however reasonable it sounds.

Refused. A kiosk is a screen that its user did not choose to stand in front of. That is a property of a surface, and the list holds media. The repair names a medium of the list.

Clean.

Two of the lists look alike, and they are kept apart on purpose.

One finding, on the message. On the screen, danger passes: SIGNALS says what a value means about a record. On the message it is refused: TONE is the register in which the system speaks, and the repair takes the tone critical. Two subjects, two lists, and a word of one is refused in the other. This is also where the red of the first refusal went: a declaration says that a value means danger, and a medium decides how danger is shown.

The decision, and what was refused

What I refused

I refused nesting. A field holds a value or a list of names. The grammar gives the reason: nesting "is where widget trees creep back into an intent language".

I refused to let any word be a medium. SURFACE_AS once accepted any name, and kiosk passed. A closed list of media is what makes a table of verbs against media finite, and a kiosk is a property of one of them.

I refused one vocabulary for the tone and the signal. The specification draws the line: one subject with two vocabularies is a defect, which the law corrected in itself, and "two subjects with two vocabularies is correct", provided the border is written down.

I refused silence on a misplaced field. Since version 1.4 of the language, on 1 November 2026, a known field on a kind that does not carry it is refused. A file that carried one was accepted the day before.

The codes above, in the words of the verifier's contract

  • UNKNOWN_FIELDlevel 1, errorA field name is not one the grammar defines in the form it is written.
  • FIELD_MISPLACEDlevel 2, errorA field is declared on a kind that does not declare it.
  • DUPLICATE_FIELDlevel 1, errorA field key appears more than once in one declaration.
  • DUPLICATE_DECLARATIONlevel 1, errorTwo declarations share a kind and a name.
  • INVALID_TONElevel 2, errorTONE outside its enumeration.

  • UNKNOWN_ROLElevel 1, errorA ROLE value is not one of the five promises this language defines.

Where the field leads

The field leads in what its descriptions can compute. SCXML describes a machine of states and of the events that move it. ALWAYS_REACHABLE states what stays within reach, and it describes no machine.

And the design tokens name what a declaration leaves to the drawing: colours, dimensions, typefaces. A team that declares in Zayn still needs those names, and the token format is where the field is writing them.

Where it stands

  • builta grammar of 10 kinds of declaration and 5 closed lists of values, specified at version 1.7; the grammar's own refusals, decided from the file alone: a field it does not know, a field on a kind that does not carry it, a field or a declaration written twice, a value outside a closed list
  • designedthe grammars of motion, message and tempo, the fields of expression that follow SIGNALS and ROLE
  • nextthe law served to an AI model while it generates

Built means that it ran on this page or runs in Zayn's repository at the commit named under the title. Designed means that it is specified, and that its build comes after. Next names the direction.

The grammar refuses what this chapter showed: a field, a place, a second copy, a value. It reads the 10 kinds it defines, it reports the words WIDGET and USER with a warning, and it passes over any other kind as another language's. Appendix B gives the grammar in full, with the form each field takes.

In your hands

Here is a declaration that the verifier accepts, and that holds four defects.

Clean! Now read the first line again, letter by letter, and repair what you find. Before you run it again, write down the codes you expect. Try before you read on.

Two refusals, and a third defect waits behind the one on the tone: the tone is on the wrong kind, and its word comes from the other list. Repair each one, and go on until the verifier answers clean and every line of your file is true.

The first draft was clean because the verifier read nothing of it: SCREN is not a kind of this language, and a kind of another language is passed over, with whatever it holds. A file may hold declarations of several languages, and the verifier judges only its own. So how is it to tell a misspelt kind of its own from a kind that belongs to someone else? The record holds two answers. The verifier passes such a kind over. The evaluator of chapter 9, forged from a second declaration of the language, takes the other course: its file says of the kinds of other languages that they are "refused, not ignored".

A declaration that the grammar accepts can still break the law. The next chapter makes the verifier refuse one, and reads the refusal line by line.

Part III · Chapter 8Spine

The refusal

Draft

Run on 2026-11-23 16:31 UTC+01:00 by the reference verifier of the zayn command, release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), against the law at version 3.17: the verifier gave the expected answer on 9 of 9 declarations.

Each declaration on this page was checked as a file by the verifier's JavaScript reference, the one the zayn command is held to, under Node 22.20.0. Every report printed below is the one that run gave. The lines that begin with //--> state the answer the page expects, and the build fails on any other.

A refusal is the verifier's answer to a declaration it does not accept: a finding that is an error. Chapter 7's refusals were for the grammar. In this chapter I make the verifier refuse for the law. I give it a declaration, I print its answer as the run gave it, and I read that answer one line at a time: what it found and where, why, and under which law. Then I repair the declaration and run it again.

If you open the book here, three words are enough to follow. A declaration is a few lines that say what a user is doing on a surface, with 22 verbs and no others, and that say nothing of how the surface is drawn. The law is Zayn's constitution for interfaces: 123 numbered rules, kept as data, under 7 articles and 6 rights of the user. The verifier is the program that reads a declaration and checks it against the law. Chapter 6 gives the verbs, chapter 7 the 10 kinds of declaration, and Part VII the law.

The field

The field refuses program code, and it has given the refusal a shape. A linter is a program that reads source code and reports what breaks its rules: it has named rules, and a severity for each. ESLint's documentation lists three severities, off, warn and error, and says of the last that the "exit code is 1 when triggered". An exit code is the number a command hands back when it ends. A build, the chain of commands that turns a team's sources into a product, reads that number and stops.

For the interface, the field speaks in three other ways, each at its own moment.

It advises. The third of Jakob Nielsen's ten heuristics, User Control and Freedom, asks for a clearly marked "emergency exit" from an unwanted action, and its tips ask for undo and redo. The page calls the ten items broad rules of thumb. A rule of thumb is read by a person and applied by judgment.

It sets criteria. WCAG 2.2, a W3C Recommendation, has a criterion, 3.3.4, for the page that commits its user to a payment or to a legal act: the submission is reversible, or it is checked, or it is confirmed. A page meets the criterion or fails it, once the page exists.

It measures. axe-core describes itself as an "accessibility testing engine" for websites, and its README puts the share of WCAG issues it finds automatically at 57 per cent on average. One step earlier, eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y checks the source of the markup before a browser renders it, and tells whoever installs it to add a tool that tests the page once rendered.

So the field refuses code by a name and an exit code. For the interface it advises, sets criteria and measures, and what its checkers read is the drawing: the markup, or the page once painted. Each of these pages was read at its source on 21 November 2026, and Appendix F lists them.

The principle

A refusal names what it refuses and in which declaration, and it cites every rule, article and right that the law holds for its code.

It does not say that something is bad practice. Where the law speaks of the defect, the refusal points at its sentence. So a refusal that cites the law has two answers and no third: repair the declaration, or amend the law with evidence. A refusal for the grammar alone, like chapter 7's unknown field, cites nothing and has one answer: the repair.

The specification of the language says why this matters: an opinion, in its words, gets "negotiated in the hallway". A finding that cites a numbered rule is settled where it can be checked: in the declaration, or in the law.

An act with no way back

Here is a payment approval as a first draft declares it. SATISFIES lists what the user does on this surface: select a payment, confirm, act. To run it yourself, save the three lines in a file and give the file to the verifier: zayn check payments.zayn. Chapter 25 installs the command, and the testbench of the Zayn site checks a declaration in the browser with nothing installed.

Two refusals, and the exit code is 1! That number is what the command hands back when it ends, and 1 means that the verifier refused. The two lines that begin with //--> are comments, which the verifier skips. They state the answer this page expects, and the book's build fails if the verifier gives another.

Read the first refusal one line at a time.

The first line is made to be scanned. It gives the file and the line, payments.zayn:1; the severity, error; the code, MISSING_UNDO; and the subject of the finding, here the name of the declaration, approve_payment. The code is the stable part. Zayn's conformance suite compares the codes a verifier reports and nothing else: the line number, the wording and the order stay outside its comparison.

The second line is the sentence. The declaration satisfies ACT, and UNDO is not among the intents it keeps reachable. The sentence names the two fields the verifier read, so you know where the repair goes.

The third line is the law: Rule 79, Article IV, the right to reverse. Three citations, and each one can be opened. Here is the rule, printed from the law's own data.

Rule 79The Undo Covenant
Article
IV · Reversibility
Set
26 · Action Reversibility
Tier
machine
Cited by
MISSING_UNDO ROLE_PROMISE_BROKEN IRREVERSIBLE_CLAIMS_UNDO
Why
Undo trusts first and interrupts never; confirmation interrupts always and trusts nothing.

Printed from the law's data, version 3.17.

And here is the right.

A right of the userThe Right to Reverse

What was done can be undone, and what cannot says so before, not after.

Printed from the law's data, version 3.17.

The rule gives its reason in one line and the right says what a user is owed. The card also names the three kinds of finding that cite this rule. The verifier checked the part of Rule 79 that a declaration states: an act, and the undo that stays within reach of it.

The second refusal has the same three lines. MISSING_CANCEL cites Rule 26, Article IV again, and another right: the right to leave. Why two refusals for one missing field? Because they protect two different moments, and the specification says which in one line: "undo reverses what was done, cancel abandons what is being done."

The last line of the report counts: two errors, no warning, one file, level 2. An error is a refusal; a warning is a finding that lets the declaration pass. Level 2 is what a verifier decides from the file alone, and chapter 9 gives the four levels.

The repair

The report said where to write: ALWAYS_REACHABLE, the field that lists what stays within the user's reach at every step.

Clean, and the exit code is 0. The report's last words give the version of the law it checked against, 3.17. I added one line. It does not say where the Cancel control sits or what the Undo looks like. It says that both stay within reach at every step.

Every finding, in one run

What does the verifier do with a declaration that breaks the law in several places? It reports every finding. Its two declarations are those of a fixture of Zayn's conformance suite. A fixture is a file kept with the answer it must get. This one has a wizard that deletes in bulk, and a message that celebrates.

Four findings in one run. Read the second line of each: it says what the verifier found.

SELECT_ACT_COLLAPSE read SATISFIES, which lists SELECT and ACT with no CONFIRM: choosing a record carries out the act. The verb CONFIRM names the user's act of confirming, whatever carries it: a review step and a dialog are two drawings of the same declaration. Rule 79's sentence on confirmation is about one drawing, the dialog that interrupts, and it keeps that dialog for acts that cannot be undone.

MISSING_UNDO is the refusal of plate 8.1.

TRAPPED_FLOW read STEPS and ALWAYS_REACHABLE. A declaration with steps is a flow of several steps, and this one keeps CANCEL within reach and no EXIT. Cancel abandons the act in progress. Exit leaves the flow. A user of this wizard can drop the deletion and stay caught in its two steps.

DECORATIVE_ANIMATION stands on the message. The verifier read its TONE and looked for REPORTS, the field that says which state a message reports. It found none. The code says animation, and it covers any feedback that moves or takes a tone and reports nothing.

Now look at the third line of each. The citations are not the same length. SELECT_ACT_COLLAPSE cites a rule and an article, and no right. TRAPPED_FLOW cites two rules. DECORATIVE_ANIMATION cites a rule and Article I. A citation is as long as the law is: the verifier prints the rules, articles and rights its contract binds to that code, and adds nothing. The contract is the list of everything the verifier can report. Of its 40 kinds of finding, 20 cite a rule by its number, 8 cite an article alone, and 12 cite nothing, because where the law has no rule the verifier claims none. A finding that cites nothing has one answer: the repair.

Here is the repair of all four.

Clean. Three verbs were added to the wizard, and the message now reports a state.

An act that cannot be undone

Some acts cannot be taken back, and purging an archive is one. Does the law ask for an undo all the same? It asks for one of two things, in the sentence that binds the 4 verbs of action, ACT, CONFIRM, CANCEL and UNDO: every act has a reachable undo, or declares why it cannot.

The language has a word for the second half. A declaration of the kind INTERACTION stands for one control, and it can state the control's role. One of its roles is irreversible. Here is a first draft that states the role and keeps the habit.

Refused, under the same Rule 79! The declaration promises a way back that the act does not have, and a user who trusts that promise learns the truth at the one moment it matters.

Under the report, the plate prints the same answer as a machine reads it, for the tools that read reports in place of people. The command gives this form when it is asked with --json. It is one object: the level, the versions of the contract and of the law, the files, the counts, and a list named diagnostics with one entry for each finding. In the entry, code is the stable name. span gives the file and the line. cites gives the law as three keys: rule:79, article:reversibility, right:reverse. subject says what the finding is about, and level says at which level it was decided. A build needs less than that. It reads the exit code: 0 when the verifier refused nothing, 1 when it refused, 2 when it could not read the file.

The repair removes the promise and keeps the right that still holds.

Clean. So an act has two lawful forms: it keeps an undo within reach, or it says that it has none. Saying nothing is refused, as plate 8.1 showed. Saying both is refused, as plate 8.5 showed.

The decision, and what was refused

What I refused

I refused a verifier that stops at the first finding. A file with four defects gets four findings in one run, as plate 8.3 shows. The suite carries that file as a fixture, and a verifier passes it only by reporting all four.

I refused to compare wording. The suite that keeps two verifiers to one verdict compares the codes they report and nothing else: the line number, the order and the sentence are free. Between the reference and its own port the bar is higher, and chapter 9 gives it. The contract binds each code to the law it cites, and the sentence may be written in whatever language its reader reads.

I refused a citation that the law does not back. A finding that cites a rule is answered by a repair or by an amendment, so a citation is a claim. The ruling of 2 November 2026 left two kinds of finding, EXPRESSION_ORPHAN and VIBE_STRIPS_RIGHT, citing an article and no rule.

The court

The court of a chapter is what proves it. Here it is Zayn's conformance suite: 77 fixtures, each a declaration kept with the answer it must get, and a manifest that lists those answers. The build ran each fixture below in the snapshot of Zayn and compared its answer with the manifest.

Of the fixtures, 28 must get no finding, because a check that fires on everything proves nothing. Among them are the lawful twins: for a refused declaration, a second fixture where the defect is repaired. The box below sets a refused fixture beside its twin wherever the suite has one.

Where the field leads

The field leads on the painted page. A checker such as axe-core reads the interface a browser has built: the contrast of a text against its background, the name a button exposes to a screen reader. Its rule list had 105 rules on 21 November 2026, each with its impact and its tags. A declaration of Zayn has no colour and no widget: both belong to the drawing. Chapter 10 measures the painted page.

And WCAG's criterion reaches the page as a user meets it, where a declaration states what every drawing of it must keep. A team keeps both: the refusal before anything is drawn, and the measurement of what was drawn.

Where it stands

  • builtthe refusal in three forms, all run on this page: the report a person reads, the machine form a tool reads and the exit code a build reads; a contract of 40 kinds of finding, 20 of them citing a rule of the law by its number; the role irreversible, with which an act says that it cannot be taken back
  • designedthe screen, the voice line or the machine surface drawn from a declaration: the verifier judges the declaration, and its drawing for each medium is designed
  • nextthe law served to an AI model while it generates, so that a generated surface cites the rules it kept

Built means that it ran on this page or runs in Zayn's repository at the commit named under the title. Designed means that it is specified, and that its build comes after. Next names the direction.

Every run on this page was made by the verifier's JavaScript reference, at Zayn's release 0.2.0, against the law at version 3.17. A refusal covers what a declaration states: on this page, what its fields say of intents, reach, steps, tone and role. The rules it cites say more than a declaration can state, and Part VII sets the law's three instruments side by side: the verifier, the audit of the painted page and a person's judgment. A clean verdict covers the declaration and what it states. Whether the declaration is true of the screen that is delivered is measured on the painted page, in chapter 10.

In your hands

Here is a wizard that closes an account, and a closed account stays closed.

Cover the report under the declaration, write the codes you expect, then compare.

Now repair it. Adding UNDO silences MISSING_UNDO and makes the declaration untrue: nothing reopens the account. The true word is irreversible. Write it on the wizard, and say what you expect.

Refused, for the place of the word: a role belongs to an interaction. Go on until the verifier answers clean and every line of your file is true. Try before you read on.

Here is a form the verifier accepts.

It is clean, and it has two declarations: the wizard, which no longer says that it acts, and an interaction that acts and says irreversible. The act had to move: irreversible is a role, and only an interaction states a role. The two stand side by side, and the file leaves their order to its reader. Should a flow be able to say that its own act cannot be undone? Or is one interaction for each such act the right grain?

A refusal is worth what the court behind it is worth. The next chapter gives the four levels, runs the suite, and tells how a second verifier, the command, is kept to the reference's verdict.

Part III · Chapter 9

One verdict, two verifiers

Draft

Run on 2026-11-23 16:32 UTC+01:00 by the reference verifier of the zayn command, release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), against the law at version 3.17: the verifier gave the expected answer on 6 of 6 declarations.

Each declaration on this page was checked as a file by the verifier's JavaScript reference, the one the zayn command is held to, under Node 22.20.0. Every report printed below is the one that run gave. The lines that begin with //--> state the answer the page expects, and the build fails on any other.

A verdict is the set of codes a verifier reports on one file. This chapter asks what keeps that verdict the same when the verifier changes. I give the four levels of checking and what each one needs. I run the conformance suite, which is a set of declarations kept with the answers they must get. Then I tell how two verifiers, written in two languages, are kept to one verdict, and how a third evaluator, made another way, keeps a list of the places where it differs.

If you open the book here: a declaration is a few lines that say what a user is doing on a surface; the law is Zayn's constitution of 123 rules for interfaces; the verifier is the program that checks a declaration against it; and a finding is one entry of the verifier's report, a refusal when it is an error. The contract is the list of every kind of finding the verifier can report, and the machine form is the same report as data.

The field

The field knows how to keep several implementations of one standard to one result: it writes a shared suite of tests. The web-platform-tests project calls itself "a cross-browser test suite for the Web-platform stack", and its results are archived from an array of web browsers on a regular basis. Test262 is, in its own words, "the implementation conformance test suite" for the specification of ECMAScript, the standard behind JavaScript.

For interfaces, the field has taken the same step for the instruments that test a page. The W3C's format for accessibility test rules, a Recommendation of 5 February 2026, asks that each rule be published with examples whose outcome is known: passed, failed, and inapplicable. It gives the purpose: the harmonization of testing methods, the ones built into test tools among them.

So the instrument is known: cases with known answers, published, and run by every implementation. Each of these pages was read at its source on 23 November 2026, and Appendix F lists them.

The principle

A verdict belongs to the suite: a fixture is a declaration kept with the answer it must get, and every verifier, in whatever language it is written, is held to that answer at the level it can see.

The page of Zayn's suite says what this is for: with it, an implementation can "prove agreement rather than assert it".

Four levels of seeing

A verifier decides only what it is given enough to see. The contract files every kind of finding at one of four levels.

LevelIts nameWhat the verifier is givenWhat it decidesKinds of finding
1Syntaxthe file alonethe grammar parses; verbs, kinds and structure are well-formed10
2Local semanticsthe file aloneeverything decidable from a single declaration -- the honest target of a standalone verifier25
3Cross-pillara symbol table of entities, actors, state and elementswhat the declaration cannot know about the system around it4
4Projectiona rendered surfacewhat only a painted page reveals; measured today by tools/ui-audit.html1

Printed from the verifier's contract, version 1.11.

Levels 1 and 2 need the file alone. The table's sentence for level 2 says "a single declaration"; its checks read the whole file, and some compare one declaration with another. Every plate of chapter 8 was decided there, and level 2 is the level the verifier runs at when none is asked. Level 3 needs something a declaration cannot hold: what the system around it contains. Here is a flow that posts an entry to a ledger, at level 2.

Clean. From the file alone, nothing says who may post the entry, and nothing says that anyone must.

Now the verifier is given one more thing: a symbol table, a small file that lists what the system holds. This one says that the system has two actors.

Refused! The same file, the same verifier, and one more input. The finding cites Rule 83 and Article V: an act with consequences names who performs it. The verifier's test is plain: a declaration whose SATISFIES holds ACT. The repair is one field.

Clean, at level 3. A table has four lists: entities, actors, state and elements. Each level 3 check waits for its own list, and a check whose list is not given says nothing. So read the words "clean at level 3" with the table in mind: they say that nothing was found among the checks the table made possible.

The suite, run on this page

A fixture is a declaration kept with the answer it must get. The suite is 77 fixtures and a manifest, the list that gives each fixture its level and the codes it must receive. The build of this book ran the suite's own runner in the snapshot of Zayn. Here is what it printed.

exit code 0run at this build by the suite's own runner, in the snapshot of Zayn

Read it from the bottom. Every fixture passed. The manifest says what a pass is: a run passes a fixture when the set of codes it reports equals the expected set, exactly. The line number, the wording of a message and the order of the findings stay outside the comparison, as chapter 8 said.

The three lines above the count are agreements the runner checks beside the fixtures. Every finding and every report has the shape of the machine form. The media the verifier knows are the ones the data lists. The contract's 40 kinds of finding are the ones the specification catalogues. The last two are each one truth kept in two places, and the runner fails when the places differ.

Now the same runner, asked for level 2.

Runnode tools/zayn/conformance.js --level 2
Zayn conformance — level 2
  spec         doc/language/ v1.7
  contract     violations.json v1.11 (constitution v3.17)
  envelope     diagnostic-contract v1.2.2 — 54 diagnostics and 72 reports, all conform

72 passed and 5 were skipped. The skipped ones are the fixtures of level 3, and a skip is not a failure: a verifier that reads the file alone has nothing with which to decide who an actor is. It states its level, and the suite holds it to that level.

A verifier written by other hands is judged the same way. It claims a level, it is run on each fixture at or below that level, and the set of codes it reports is compared with the manifest's. The manifest gives each fixture its file, its level, the codes it must get and, at level 3, its symbol table.

Of the 77 fixtures, 28 must get no finding, and 23 of those are lawful twins of a fixture that gets a finding. And 3 kinds of finding have no fixture at all, each with its reason written in the manifest. One is the finding of level 4, which is a fact about a painted page. The other two are failures to parse: what a parser reports after its first failure differs from one parser to the next, and a fixture would bind every verifier to one parser's habits.

The suite holds no fixture above level 3, so its last line at level 4 says what a run at level 3 says. Level 4 needs a painted page, and chapter 10 measures one.

Two verifiers, one answer

The verifier that ran every page of this book is written in JavaScript. It is the reference.

The verifier a team installs is the zayn command, one file, written in another language. It is a port of the reference: the same verifier, written again. Its bar is set above the suite's. The suite compares codes. A gate is a check that must pass before a release, and the gate between the command and the reference compares every byte: what each prints, what each prints on failure, and the exit code, on every fixture and on a corpus, a large set of inputs that a program makes from the fixtures. The first lines of the gate's file state its rule: "There are NO allowed differences."

Why bytes, when the suite asks only for codes? The design of the command answers: a port that agrees on the codes and differs in a message "has changed what a person reads".

I asked for that command in these words, which the design keeps as I typed them: "We should not depend on Node or any other thing!" Node is the program that runs JavaScript.

The release notes record the runs. Those of release 0.1.0 record the gate's full run with no difference to the byte. Those of release 0.2.0 record the Windows file passing the suite, 77 fixtures of 77, and list the Linux and macOS files as built.

The same core is also compiled for the browser, 134584 bytes, so that a page can check a declaration with nothing installed. A proof page runs every fixture at every level through it and compares each answer with the command's: the record it compares with holds 308 answers for 77 fixtures.

The first lines of the gate's file also say what it proves, and I keep the sentence beside the result: "Parity is sameness, not rightness". A command that agrees with the reference on every input carries every mistake of the reference.

A third evaluator, and its differences

Two verifiers that share a design can share a blind spot. So the language itself was also written down a second time, in Haro, the language of this series' first book, which is a language for declaring languages. The declaration was written from the contract's data and the tables of the declarations. An evaluator is forged from that declaration, which means that a program makes it from the declaration with no hand in between, and it shares no code with the verifier.

It does not agree everywhere, and that is its use. A script compares the two. It ran the forged evaluator against the reference on 73 fixtures. The list of its differences holds 22 rows, four of them added on 8 November 2026 for the menu fixtures and written by expectation: from what the evaluator is expected to say, ahead of the run that confirms it. Each row names the fixture, what each of the two says, and the class of the difference. In 9 rows both refuse and speak different codes. In 3 rows the forged evaluator refuses a file the verifier accepts. In 10 rows the verifier refuses or warns and the forged evaluator says clean, and the 5 fixtures of level 3 are among them. The script counts a fixture as agreed when the forged evaluator's first code is one of the codes expected: it speaks one refusal for a file, where the verifier reports them all. It also refuses the kinds of other languages, which the verifier passes over: the difference that chapter 7's exercise met.

The list is a ratchet, a list that may only shrink. The script fails when a difference appears that is not on it, when a listed row changes, and when a listed difference now agrees and is still listed. A difference can leave the list only by being repaired and removed.

The decision, and what was refused

What I refused

I refused to choose where the verifier lives before there was evidence. The decision document of 6 August 2026 sets the order: the fixtures and the specification first, before a verifier could pass them. Once a suite exists, two implementations that drift apart are a failing run.

I refused to fail a fixture that a verifier cannot see. A fixture above a verifier's level is skipped. A verifier that pretended to decide it would be claiming a level it does not have.

I refused a fixture for what a declaration cannot show. The finding of level 4 is a fact about a painted page. The manifest says of a fixture for it that it "would be theatre".

I refused a table that the verifier computes. A verifier that stands alone accepts the symbol table as an input. What the system around a declaration holds is that system's to say.

Where the field leads

The field leads in the number of hands. The web's suite is written to run in all browsers, and the results of an array of them are archived. Zayn's record holds one reference, one port of it in two builds, and one evaluator made another way, whose comparing script runs where the Haro forge is installed. The direction is the field's: more verifiers, written by other hands, each stating its level and listing its differences.

The field also has a third outcome beside passed and failed: inapplicable, the nearest thing to this suite's skip.

And a suite proves agreement. Whether what the verifiers agree on is right is the law's business, and Part VII's.

Part VII · Chapter 16

The constitution, part by part

Draft

Run on 2026-11-23 16:32 UTC+01:00 by the reference verifier of the zayn command, release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), against the law at version 3.17: the verifier gave the expected answer on 11 of 11 declarations.

Each declaration on this page was checked as a file by the verifier's JavaScript reference, the one the zayn command is held to, under Node 22.20.0. Every report printed below is the one that run gave. The lines that begin with //--> state the answer the page expects, and the build fails on any other.

The constitution of Zayn is one file. In this chapter I open that file and read it part by part: what it says of itself, its articles, its sets, one rule field by field, the rights of the user and the rules that enforce each, the patterns it forbids. Then I make the verifier refuse three declarations, and I follow each citation back into the file.

If you open the book here, four words are enough to follow. A declaration is a few lines that say what a user is doing on a surface. The law is Zayn's constitution for interfaces. The verifier is the program that checks a declaration against the law. A finding is one entry of the verifier's report, and a refusal when it is an error.

The field

The field writes its rules as documents, in layers. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines are organised around "four principles", with "a total of 13 guidelines" under them, and under each guideline come success criteria, numbered like 3.3.4 and "written as testable criteria". A classic of the field is a list: ten heuristics of usability, each a name and a paragraph, which their page calls "broad rules of thumb".

For the people who test a page, the ACT Rules Format says what a test rule must state. Two of its parts are the applicability, "what parts of the test subject are tested", and the expectations, each of which is "an assertion about a test target".

And the field keeps some of its decisions as data. The Design Tokens format defines a token as information with "a human readable name": a colour, a dimension, a typeface. Those are values of the drawing.

So the field has documents in layers, lists of advice, a format for a rule that a tester runs, and data for the values of a drawing. Each source was read on 21 or 23 November 2026, and Appendix F lists them.

The principle

The law is one file: the page that shows it, the count that sizes it and the refusal that cites it all read it there.

The file is named rules.json. It is written in a notation for data, names and values between braces, and a designer reads the law on a page that is drawn from it, never in the notation. The verifier reads the same file at each run: the title of a rule and the numeral of an article in a report are looked up there. Every count on this page is read from it by the book's build. Appendix A prints it in full.

What the file says of itself

The file opens on its title, its version and its lineage, the dated list of its changes that chapter 18 reads. Then comes a preamble. It says what the law is for: "non-negotiable principles for business interfaces", which it wants "framework-agnostic, trend-resistant, and machine-checkable". It names its subject once: "the operator and the user name whoever acts through an interface: the user, a person or an agent". And it closes on four sentences, of which the last is "Undo is dignity."

The word philosophy names two things in the file. One is a line of four phrases, each of the form "X Over Y": calm over power, intent over mechanics, visible over hidden, business over technology. 4 of the articles carry one of them as their axiom. The other is a part of 3 principles, which stand before the articles and outside the count of rules.

The articles

An article is a sentence of principle, and every rule derives from one article: each of the 123 rules names it in a field, derived_from. Here are the articles, with the number of rules that derive from each.

ArticleIts titleIts sentenceRules derived from it
ICalmThe interface must never compete with the operator’s thinking. Calm is a functional requirement, not an aesthetic choice — anything that draws attention without serving intent does not belong, whether it is drawn by a designer or spoken by a machine.34
IIIntent Over MechanicsInteraction starts from what the human is trying to do — discover, focus, read, select, act, recover — and widgets are consequences of intent, never primitives. Selection never implies execution; a flow that traps is unconstitutional.17
IIIVisible StateIf the system knows something important, the user must see it: active filters, pending drafts, norms, background work, and machine provenance alike. Invisible state is a violation.24
IVReversibilityUndo is dignity. Every act is reversible, or explicitly and visibly irreversible — staged, named, and reviewed. Configuration never commits itself, and the way back is never broken.4
VPredictable AuthorityEvery consequential act names its actor, every claimed role is declared, and the same control always means the same thing. An intelligent agent is an actor under this law — never an authority above it.6
VIOperator Primacy and VibesBusiness users are operators, not explorers, and their culture deserves architectural respect: vibes, densities, dialects, and surfaces are equivalent vibes of one truth. Vibe-invariant rights never flex.37
VIIAmendmentThe law grows only from evidence: real usage, operator feedback, documented failure analysis. Removing a protection requires proof the harm is gone; adding one requires proof the harm is real and recurring. Trends, fashion, and developer convenience are not grounds. Retired numbers are never reused.1

Printed from the law's data, version 3.17.

The counts are uneven, and that is information. Most rules protect calm, visible state and the culture of the people who use an interface. Reversibility needs few rules, and the article on amendment fewest of all.

One rule, field by field

Every rule has the same shape. Here is Rule 105, whole, as the file holds it.

Field, as the file names itWhat this rule holds
idthe-legibility-floor
number105
titleThe Legibility Floor
avoidBody text below 1rem; Muted grays that fail 4.5:1 contrast against their background; Accent-colored text that fails contrast on light backgrounds; Meaning conveyed by faintness
solutionMain reading text is at least 1rem with generous line height, and never lighter than 4.5:1 against its background; long-form prose aims for 7:1. Secondary text may be quieter in size or weight -- never in legibility. If a color carries meaning, it must also carry contrast.
whyText you must lean into is text you will misread -- faintness is not a design language, it is a tax on every reader.
derived_fromoperator
enforcementtool
invarianttrue
evidenceAmended in v2.1 after the framework's own site shipped small, low-contrast muted text -- observed by the author, fixed the same day. Amendment by documented failure analysis, exactly as Article VII demands.
lintmeasured by tools/ui-audit.html: computed size and true contrast, every text node, both vibes

Printed from the law's data, version 3.17.

9 fields are on every rule. id is a handle, and number is what a citation carries. title is the name printed after the number in a report. avoid is a list of defects, and solution is the text of the rule: together they make a rule something a reviewer can decide, yes or no. why is the reason in a sentence or two. derived_from is the article. enforcement is one of four words, the rule's tier, and chapter 17 is about them. evidence says what earned the rule its number; the site in Rule 105's evidence is the one that carried the law at the time.

5 fields are on some rules. invariant is a mark, the value true, on 47 rules: the page that shows the law prints it as the badge "vibe-invariant", and Article VI uses the same word of rights: "Vibe-invariant rights never flex." A vibe is a culture of interaction, and chapter 15 is about it. lint is a sentence that names a check or an instrument, on 18 rules. vibes holds a note for one culture or another, on 14. see_also points at a neighbouring rule, on 7. absorbs names the retired number that a rule took in, on 5.

A right is a sentence about the user, and it lists the rules that enforce it.

RightIts sentenceRules that enforce it
The Right to UnderstandEvery element, denial, and setting can explain itself in the operator’s language.40, 42, 71, 86, 99
The Right to ReverseWhat was done can be undone, and what cannot says so before, not after.26, 70, 79, 93
The Right to KnowThe state of the system — filters, drafts, progress, provenance — is always visible.13, 24, 25, 29, 37, 57, 58, 59, 81, 82, 99
The Right to LeaveEvery flow, focus, and overlay has a reachable exit that returns the user to where they stood.26, 51, 53, 92, 93
The Right to Act Without FearNo element creates anxiety through unpredictability, irreversibility by default, or hidden consequences.15, 18, 19, 38, 79, 83, 89, 91
The Right to a HumanWherever a machine serves, a person is reachable — clearly, and without penalty.102

The decision, and what was refused

What I refused

The law refuses a second use of a number. Article VII ends on it: "Retired numbers are never reused." Two numbers that an earlier numbering had used for other things are marked in the file with these words: "Reserved, never to be assigned". A citation of Rule 79 names the same rule in every version of the law.

An amended rule keeps its number. When Rule 116 was first amended, on 5 August 2026, the lineage wrote: "No new number: the same rule, stated whole." A rule that changes is the same rule, with its history in its evidence.

I refused to cite a standard before reading it. In my pass of 13 August 2026 a proposal asked to add to a rule the standards that corroborate it. I adopted it as a commission, and the docket, the file where changes to the law are ruled, keeps the condition: "nothing is written into rules.json" until the editions of those standards are read and their clauses recorded.

I kept the law's role word. The law says operator where this book says user. On 7 November 2026 I ruled that the law's prose names its subject as the user, a person or an agent. The word operator stayed in the rules and in the title of Article VI, and the docket says why: "it is the law's role word, not a description of a human". One definition in the preamble now makes every use of it mean the user.

Where the field leads

The field leads on what stands behind a criterion. The criterion read for chapter 8 has a page of its own, which states its intent, and every criterion is "written as testable". Zayn's oldest rules share one line of evidence, and the rules canonized since version 2.1 each carry their own event.

Zayn's law leads on being read by tools. A count, a citation and a page all come from one file, so a rule's number means one thing wherever it is printed. The cost is on the other side of the file: a text written by hand beside it can differ from it, and the ledger, the dated list of what the project found, says so in one line: "a number in prose is attached to nothing that can contradict it". This book takes the remedy that the ledger gives: its counts are read from the file at each build.

And a list has no order of rank. Two rules can speak of one subject, and chapter 18 tells how one such pair was reconciled.

Where it stands

  • builtthe law as one data file at version 3.17: a preamble, 7 articles, 6 rights, 17 forbidden patterns and 31 sets of 123 rules; citations made of the file's own numbers and names, run on this page; a page that shows the whole law, drawn from the file; the file held by its hash in a pack of 12 files
  • designeda law in four parts, from a core that every interface keeps to a commons that teams add to; a field on a rule that records the sources which corroborate it
  • nextthe law served to AI tools as they work, and rules moved to an instrument as each instrument is built

Built means that it ran on this page or runs in Zayn's repository at the commit named under the title. Designed means that it is specified, and that its build comes after. Next names the direction.

Every table of this page was printed from the law's file at version 3.17, and every citation was run. What reads the file at that version is the verifier, for the titles and the numerals of a report; the page that shows the law, for every part; the site, for its figures; and the pack, for the hash. The rights' lists name rules up to number 102, and whether a newer rule joins a list is a question for a pass, a sitting where changes to the law are ruled. A report prints the article that its kind of finding is bound to, which for most is the article of the rule it cites.

Cover the report under the declaration, write the codes you expect and how many, then compare. Four findings of one code: a printed page carries none of the four verbs. The first repair most readers try is to change the act into reading. Say what you expect.

Three stay: a page cannot keep within reach what it cannot carry. Go on until the verifier answers clean and every line of your file is true. Try before you read on.

Clean. Now do what this chapter did: follow the citation of the first report into the file. The report says Rule 82 and Article II, and names no right. In the file, Rule 82 derives from Article III, and the right to know lists it. So when a refusal cites a rule, does it answer to that rule's article and to the right the rule serves, or to an article of its own? The contract binds this kind of finding to Article II, and its note says why it cites Rule 82: that rule "is what made 'the declared medium' a legal concept". It is a remark for the law, filed with the book's findings.

A rule's card names its tier in one word. The next chapter reads those four words, and counts which rules an instrument refuses.

Part VII · Chapter 18

Amendment from evidence

Draft

Run on 2026-11-23 16:32 UTC+01:00 by the reference verifier of the zayn command, release v0.2.0 (commit adaecc271), against the law at version 3.17: the verifier gave the expected answer on 9 of 9 declarations.

Each declaration on this page was checked as a file by the verifier's JavaScript reference, the one the zayn command is held to, under Node 22.20.0. Every report printed below is the one that run gave. The lines that begin with //--> state the answer the page expects, and the build fails on any other.

An amendment is a change to what the law requires. In this chapter I tell how Zayn's law changes. I read its history in the file that holds it. I give three cases from the record: a correction of a screen that turned out to be law already, two rules that contradicted each other, and a check that ran before a rule was written for it. Then I list what moves when one rule moves.

If you open the book here, four words are enough to follow. A declaration is a few lines that say what a user is doing on a surface. The law is Zayn's constitution of 123 rules for interfaces, kept as a data file. The verifier is the program that checks a declaration against the law. A finding is one entry of the verifier's report, and a refusal when it is an error.

The field

The field amends its standards by versions. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines are at version 2.2, a W3C Recommendation. Its page lists the success criteria that are new in 2.2, and W3C's page on what is new says that the criteria of 2.0 and 2.1 are "essentially the same in 2.2, with one exception": criterion 4.1.1, which is "obsolete and removed". The standard prints the reason under the criterion's number: assistive technology "no longer has any need to directly parse HTML". The number stays on the page, with its note.

The W3C Process Document says how a Recommendation changes after it is published. It names a correction and an addition, and calls the two together "candidate amendments".

A regulation can then name one version. The fact sheet of the United States rule on the web content of state and local governments names "Version 2.1, Level AA" as its technical standard, with dates of compliance in April 2027 and April 2028.

A design system grows by criteria. The GOV.UK Design System asks of a proposal that there be evidence it would be "useful for many teams or services", and that it be unique. A linter, which is a tool that checks source code against rules, does the same for its rules: ESLint lists guidelines for a rule of its core, and says that since 2020 it accepts a new one only for a new feature of the language it checks.

And the field has a convention for what a version number promises. Semantic Versioning moves the first number when a change breaks what relied on the version before, the second for what is added, the third for a fix.

So the field amends by versions, admits by criteria, and keeps a removed number on its page. Each source was read on 23 November 2026, and Appendix F lists them.

The principle

The law changes only on evidence, and every change stays on the record: its date, its cause, and what it replaced.

The law says so itself, in its last article.

Article VIIAmendment

The law grows only from evidence: real usage, operator feedback, documented failure analysis. Removing a protection requires proof the harm is gone; adding one requires proof the harm is real and recurring. Trends, fashion, and developer convenience are not grounds. Retired numbers are never reused.

Printed from the law's data, version 3.17.

The article sets two burdens. To add a protection, the harm must be shown. To remove one, the harm must be shown to be gone. It names what is not a ground. And its last sentence is about numbers: a rule's number is a name, and a name that is given twice means two things.

The law's history, in its file

The law carries its history with it. The lineage is a list of dated entries, one for each state of the law: 32 entries, from version 2.0 on 3 August 2026 to version 3.17 on 12 November 2026. Most entries canonize a rule, which means that they give it a number and a place in a set. Some amend a rule and add none. Some are corrections of wording. Some change a word or a name.

What tells an amendment from a correction of wording? One question. The document that sets the law's architecture calls it the substance test: "does any interface that was lawful before become unlawful after — or must any conforming implementation change anything it does?" A conforming implementation is a tool that keeps to the law. If the answer is no, the change is a correction, "however much prose changed". The first entry of 6 August 2026 is one: two lines of the law named a file that had moved, and no requirement moved with them.

The numbers have a history too. The rules are numbered up to 130 and the law holds 123, so 7 numbers are out of use. 5 are retired: each was a duplicate, folded into the rule that survives it, and the survivor says which number it absorbed. 2 are reserved for good, because older documents had cited them for something else. A number that is only proposed can be taken too. The docket is the file where changes to the law are proposed together and ruled item by item, in sittings that it calls passes. It had kept the number 125 for a candidate when another rule was written under it, and that rule became Rule 126. The docket's lesson: "a proposed number is not a free number".

Each of the 123 rules carries a field named evidence: what happened, where and when. Since version 3.13, an amended rule keeps its first evidence and gains a dated clause after it. The architecture document gives the rule for that field in four words: "Evidence is never corrected." What happened stays as it was written.

A correction that was already law

In August 2026 an AI agent that was not consulting the law built a status dashboard for me. I rejected two versions and corrected the third. The ledger is the dated list of what the project found, and it says what those corrections were worth: "Every correction he made was already law."

The first version was a grid of tiles, and the second was cards with coloured meters. My words, as the ledger keeps them: "use a classical table format not cards, it's more direct and less stressing to me". Rule 119 and Rule 94 already forbade both. Then came two red blocks, one under the other. Mine again: "having two red divs one under the other means we are not focusing on one critical thing." That was Rule 87. Then every table was wrapped in a container that scrolls sideways, which Rule 14 forbids. When that was removed, each row was stacked into a block, which is the first thing that Rule 95, a rule of the field culture, tells its reader to avoid.

So what did the episode add to the law? Five candidates were put to the docket on 15 August 2026. Two were refused as new law, because each was a rule that existed, and each of those rules was extended by a sentence. Three were canonized, and Rule 129 is one of them. The column that the scrollbar hid had carried my next action. The law forbade the scrollbar. It did not say "which column survives when width genuinely runs out", and that is the whole of the new rule.

Why is this evidence, and not compliance? Because the law was closed while it happened. The ledger's sentence names the law's file: "Nobody consulted rules.json while it happened". The docket gives the size of the case, "one surface, one operator, one implementer", and I print it at that size.

Two rules that contradicted each other

On 16 August 2026 Rule 3 and Rule 118 were put side by side: for the first time, by the ledger's account. Both speak of colour. Rule 3 kept the colour of danger for a failure of the system. Rule 118 gives danger to a value that is critical or exceeded. So a credit limit that is exceeded, coloured as danger, obeyed one rule and broke the other.

Which rule outranks the other? Neither: the ledger records that the law has "no precedence mechanism at all". I had delegated that pass to an AI agent, and the docket records it as a delegation. The pass invented no rule of precedence. On the colour of danger it gave the subject to Rule 118, "on the merits, not by seniority", and it amended both rules until they no longer overlapped: "Rule 3 owns chrome. Rule 118 owns what a colour means about a record." Chrome is the frame of an interface: its bars, its borders, its controls. Each rule now points at the other in a field named see_also, and 7 rules carry such a pointer.

The language took Rule 118's statuses the same day, as the closed list of the field SIGNALS. Here is a screen that uses two words of chrome as statuses.

Two refusals, and both cite Rule 118. The word danger passes. The other two belong to the frame, and the frame is Rule 3's. Here is Rule 118 as it stands after the amendment.
